title: Packages and repositories
subtitle: Install software from signed repositories, inspect what owns a file, and undo a transaction.
objectives: Explain the roles of DNF and RPM
Install, remove, and update software with DNF
Query installed files and verify package integrity
Use transaction history to understand or reverse a change

commands.desc: Show package metadata and source repository.
Find a package that supplies a file or command.
Install a package and its dependencies.
Remove a package and unneeded dependencies.
Verify installed files against package metadata.

lab.title: Trace a package end to end
lab.scenario: Install a web server from a trusted repository, inspect exactly what it placed on disk, then remove it cleanly.

steps.text: Confirm repositories are available and locate httpd.
steps.verify: Note the repository name, version, and architecture.

steps.text: Install httpd, reading the transaction summary before confirming.
steps.verify: Review the transaction summary, confirm with y, and dnf should report httpd installed.

steps.text: Find the package owner of the main binary and list package files.
steps.verify: rpm -qf should name httpd, and rpm -ql should list the files it owns.

steps.text: Query the service unit and configuration file ownership.
steps.verify: The output should include the httpd systemd unit and httpd.conf paths.

steps.text: Review the transaction history and remove the package.
steps.cmd: dnf history | head && sudo dnf remove httpd
steps.verify: dnf history should show the install; after removal, rpm -q httpd should report not installed.

quiz.q: Which command finds the installed package that owns /usr/sbin/sshd?
quiz.why: rpm -qf queries the RPM database for the owning package. dnf provides works for available packages too.

quiz.q: What is the safest first step before a large dnf update?
options: Review check-update and the transaction, and ensure a rollback path
quiz.why: Preview the change and know how to recover. Disabling signature checks is never the answer.

options: A record of package transactions with IDs
quiz.why: DNF transactions are recorded with IDs, users, and package changes, enabling inspection and attempted undo.
